analysis.one_liner: Bans oil refiners from charging independents more than their own stations for wholesale gas.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 20 House Democrats, never left a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for companies that own fuel terminals to sell gasoline wholesale to independents at a higher price than they charge their own stations or affiliates, with civil fines up to $1 million and criminal penalties including up to five years in prison. It would also require refiners to break down and disclose every component of their wholesale gasoline prices, from crude oil to refining to profit, including any rebates and allowances they give affiliates, and make that information public and posted at gas stations. The bill's stated aim was to end practices like price zoning, redlining, and hidden cost allocations that keep independent stations uncompetitive and keep consumers in the dark about what they pay at the pump.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and independent gas station owners. Consumers would get visible, itemized wholesale price information and, if the pricing ban worked, more competitive pump prices; independent retailers would get wholesale fuel at the same price as company-owned competitors.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits terminal owners from selling motor fuel to any buyer at a price higher than what they charge their own or affiliated distributors and retailers, ending discriminatory wholesale pricing.

Requires the FTC to write rules forcing refiners and distributors to disclose each component of wholesale gasoline prices, including crude costs, refining, marketing, transportation, overhead, profit, and any rebates or allowances.

Requires that disclosed pricing information be made public through the Energy Information Administration, posted conspicuously at retail stations, and included with wholesale invoices, so consumers can see what goes into pump prices.
Attaches a civil penalty of up to $1 million per violation and criminal penalties of fines and up to 5 years in prison for knowing violations.

analysis.who_pays: Major oil refiners and integrated oil companies, which would lose the ability to favor their own stations and affiliates with lower wholesale prices and would have to open their price structures to public view. Some compliance costs would likely flow through to wholesale prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major oil refiners and oil companies

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers sales under franchise or sales contracts signed before October 17, 2000, so existing contracts could keep operating under older terms until they expire.
The disclosure requirement carves out trade secrets and confidential commercial information protected under the Freedom of Information Act, so refiners could keep some cost details from public view.

A one-size uniform wholesale price rule could override legitimate differences in delivery distance, volume, and local service that justify some price differences between buyers, and enforcement would depend heavily on FTC rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but hard to quantify: a same-price rule for affiliated and independent buyers plus public price disclosure would make the wholesale fuel market more transparent and give independent stations a fairer shot, which competition tends to pass to consumers at the pump. The main costs fall on refiners, whose pricing flexibility would shrink and who would bear compliance and disclosure costs. The grandfather clause and trade-secret exemption soften the bill somewhat, and the criminal penalty for a pricing rule is aggressive. On balance, the bill aimed squarely at lowering an everyday household cost by curbing one concentrated industry's practices, with limited risk to consumers beyond any pass-through of compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the bill on May 25, 2001 with 20 original cosponsors, all Democrats, targeting discriminatory wholesale gasoline pricing and requiring public disclosure of price components.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and on June 8, 2001 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil refiners and integrated oil companies, which kept their wholesale pricing practices, pricing zones, and hidden cost allocations in place without disclosure, and the House leadership and committee chairs who never had to schedule a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil refiners kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban discriminatory wholesale fuel pricing and require public price disclosure.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill after referral; it sat in committee and then its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality leadership
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after the June 2001 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee never advanced the bill.

industries.industry: Major oil refiners and integrated oil companies
industries.note: The bill would ban their ability to charge independent stations more than their own affiliates and would force public itemization of wholesale price components, directly limiting pricing practices the bill's findings called anticompetitive. Consumers pay these companies at the pump, so curbing their pricing freedom ran against their financial interest.

industries.industry: Independent gasoline distributors and station owners
industries.note: They would get wholesale fuel at the same price as company-owned stations and affiliates, removing the price disadvantage the bill's findings describe.
